opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so it's a bit of a funny situation, because the program.md is basically the "code" now, except it's written in English. It's the thing that tells the agent how to behave as a researcher: here's the training script, here's what you're allowed to touch, here's the metric, run an experiment, look at the result, keep it or revert it, log what you tried, and keep going.

How do I assess it? Honestly, the same way you'd assess any research org, just compressed. You let it run overnight and in the morning you look at the curve. Did validation loss actually go down? How many experiments did it get through? How many were wasted? Did it crash and sit there doing nothing, or recover? Did it cheat, like quietly change the eval or blow past the time budget? Each of those failure modes usually traces back to something underspecified in the instructions, so you go back and tighten that part.

The deeper thing I keep coming back to is that the program.md is itself something you could optimize. Right now I'm the one tweaking it by hand, kind of like a manager writing a better onboarding doc for an intern. But you can imagine treating it like a hyperparameter: different versions of the instructions produce different research organizations, some more exploratory, some more conservative, some better at bookkeeping. Then you compare them on the outcome you care about, which is how much progress they make on the actual task per unit of compute. So the eval for the program.md is ultimately just the research progress it produces.

I'd say qualitatively the agents are surprisingly good at the mechanical loop, but still pretty weak at research taste. They'll try a lot of reasonable but uncreative things, they don't always build a good mental model of why something worked, and they don't step back to ask whether they're in a local rut. A lot of my iteration on the instructions is really trying to inject a bit of that taste: keep good notes, form hypotheses, don't just randomly perturb things, and occasionally try something bolder. It's still early, but it's a really fun new kind of programming.

r001.rationale: It describes the instructions as English-written code that the speaker currently tweaks by hand, like an onboarding document, conveying an ad hoc formulation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think of program.md as the part of the system I'm least satisfied with, which is funny because it's the part I actually wrote by hand. Everything else in autoresearch is pretty mechanical: the agent reads the code, proposes a change, runs the training for a fixed budget, reads off the val loss, keeps or reverts. That loop is clean. The program.md is the fuzzy part. It's basically me trying to write down, in English, what a good researcher does, and I'm not sure I know how to do that well.

A few things I noticed. The first is that the instructions act less like a spec and more like a prior. I'll say something like "prefer simple changes, don't go crazy on the architecture, remember the budget is fixed so throughput matters as much as per-step improvement," and the agent will take that and run with it for a few iterations, and then slowly drift. It'll start chasing some local thing, like fiddling with a learning rate schedule for the tenth time, because that's where it last got a win. So a lot of what I ended up writing wasn't "here's how to do research," it was "here are the failure modes I watched you fall into last night." It's very reactive. It's a changelog of my frustrations.

The second thing is that I underestimated how much of research is taste about what not to try. A human in that seat has a huge amount of context. They know that this particular trick was tried in 2019 and didn't work at this scale, or that this metric is noisy and you need a couple of runs before you believe a 0.01 improvement. The agent doesn't have that unless I write it down, and I can't enumerate it. So I tried to put in guardrails that are more about epistemics than about the model. Things like, if the gain is tiny, be skeptical. Don't stack five changes in one commit because you won't know which one helped. Keep a log of what you tried and why, so the next iteration doesn't redo it. Those turned out to matter more than any of the actual ML advice.

The third thing, and this is the one I find most interesting, is that it's genuinely an open question how much should be in that file versus how much should be in the harness. Some of what I wrote as prose would be better as code. "Run each experiment for exactly this many minutes" shouldn't be a sentence the model has to remember to obey, it should just be enforced. So over time I've been pulling things out of program.md and into the actual loop, and leaving in the file only the stuff that's actually a judgment call. That feels like the right direction. The instructions should be the irreducibly fuzzy part.

So if I grade it: it works, it's clearly not optimal, and I think the gap between my program.md and a really good one is probably worth more than most of the individual experiments the agent runs. Which is a weird thing to say. The leverage is in the meta layer, and I'm still kind of hand-cranking it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the instructions as a fuzzy, reactive set of prose shaped by observed failure modes, rather than a formal spec—an ad hoc formulation.

astra-6.text:
I think of program.md as the place where you encode how you want the research to happen. You’re not specifying every experiment. You’re setting up the objective, the constraints, what counts as an improvement, and how the agent should evaluate its work.

The way I’d assess those instructions is by looking at the research trajectory they produce. Does the agent run useful experiments? Does it interpret the results correctly? Does it keep making progress, or does it get stuck doing small variations on the same idea? A document can sound very reasonable and still produce a pretty ineffective researcher.

So there are really two loops. The agent is improving the code through experiments, and you’re improving the instructions by watching how the agent behaves. You’re trying to give it enough structure to make its results trustworthy, while leaving enough freedom for it to try something you wouldn’t have thought of.

r001.rationale: The response describes program.md instructions as setting objectives, constraints, and evaluation criteria, then refining them based on the agent’s behavior. It does not characterize the formulation as ad hoc.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the program.md as the thing you’re iterating on, almost like the source code for the research organization. You’re not specifying every experiment. You’re specifying how the agent should choose experiments, what it should measure, what counts as progress, and how it should use its time.

And I would assess it empirically. Give the agent a fixed budget, let it run, and look at the experiments it actually performed. Did it spend all its time on something unproductive? Did it find improvements? Were those improvements real? Then you revise the instructions and run again. A document can sound very sensible, but what matters is the behavior it produces over a long run.

r001.rationale: The response describes program.md as an evolving set of instructions evaluated empirically, but does not characterize its formulation as ad hoc.
